stories.title: ULI Names Nine Developments as Americas Awards for Excellence Winners
stories.excerpt: Nine developments from across the Americas have been selected as winners of the Urban Land Institute’s (ULI’s) 2026 ULI Americas Awards for Excellence. From 93 projects and programs submitted, the 15-member jury, composed of development, finance, planning, and varied design experts, selected 16 finalists and ultimately nine winners. The 2026 ULI Americas Awards for Excellence winners include: Highland Phase II, Austin, Texas With creative financing and extensive community engagement, Highland Phase II offers a replicable model for converting dormant malls into vibrant, mixed-use community anchors. Highland Phase II transformed a vacant shopping mall into Austin Community College’s flagship 5,000-student campus. The 420,000-square-foot adaptive reuse project incorporates salvaged building components, including structural steel, to create specialized spaces informed by input from over 16 departments. The newly designed Paseo breaks down the mall’s former pedestrian barriers to improve walkability and public access. Line 5 Eglinton, Toronto, Ontario Line 5 Eglinton is Toronto’s largest transit expansion in decades, weaving 11.8 miles and 25 stations to link 22 communities along a vital east-west spine. The high-demand line connects to 54 bus routes, three subway stations, and two GO rail lines, and is projected to serve around 123,200 daily passengers by 2027. Each station integrates seamlessly with its surrounding neighborhood, while passive ventilation, adaptable entrances, and natural-light canopies are shared across the transit line. Mission Rock Phase One, San Francisco, California Raised to accommodate 66 inches of sea level rise, the project sets a new standard for resilient waterfront development. Mission Rock Phase One converted a former industrial waterfront and surface parking lot into a vibrant publicly accessible neighborhood. bullets: ULI named 9 winners from 93 submissions; Highland Phase II (Austin) converts defunct mall to ACC campus.
Line 5 Eglinton (Toronto) expands 11.8 miles, 25 stations; projected 123,200 daily riders by 2027.
Adaptive reuse and transit-oriented development models recognized for community engagement and walkability improvements.
stories.summary: The Urban Land Institute selected nine development winners across the Americas, including Highland Phase II in Austin—a 420,000-sq-ft adaptive reuse converting a vacant mall into a 5,000-student ACC campus—and Toronto's Line 5 Eglinton, an 11.8-mile transit expansion serving 25 stations and connecting 22 communities. Both projects employed creative financing and extensive public engagement. The awards highlight successful models for transforming underutilized assets and linking regional growth corridors.
stories.impact: Transit-adjacent and adaptive reuse projects signal regulatory and market appetite for mixed-use density. In Austin and Toronto, major transit expansion and campus relocations will concentrate job and student population growth near these corridors, strengthening demand fundamentals for multifamily infill development in stations zones and surrounding neighborhoods over the next 3–5 years.

stories.title: AI Tech Firm Treeswift Signs Four-Year Lease for New Manhattan Headquarters
stories.excerpt: Lee & Associates NYC announced that Treeswift Inc., an AI-powered infrastructure technology company helping electric utilities modernize field operations, has relocated its New York headquarters to 256 W. 38th St. after signing a four-year, full-floor lease for 7,487 square feet. The Philadelphia-based tenant is expected to move into its new Midtown Manhattan headquarters in August. Daniel Rodriguez of Buchbinder Warren LLC represented Treeswift. Todd Korren, Principal, Executive Managing Director, and Noah Caspi of Lee NYC represented the landlord, Hakimian Organization. Treeswift develops AI-powered software, LiDAR and sensor technology that helps electric utilities collect and analyze field data to improve infrastructure inspections, vegetation management, construction planning, wildfire mitigation and storm response. “Artificial intelligence companies have become one of the most active drivers of office leasing demand in Manhattan, but they are not all looking for trophy towers,” said Korren. “As these businesses grow, they are seeking efficient, well-connected headquarters that support collaboration, attract talent and provide long-term value. Treeswift’s relocation reflects that trend.” The post AI Tech Firm Treeswift Signs Four-Year Lease for New Manhattan Headquarters appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Treeswift (AI infrastructure firm) relocates HQ from Philadelphia to Manhattan; 7,487-sq-ft four-year lease.
Lease to 256 W. 38th St., Midtown; move-in August 2025; full-floor deal.
Signals AI/tech tenants driving efficient office leasing demand outside trophy towers in Manhattan.
stories.summary: Treeswift Inc., an AI-powered infrastructure technology company, signed a four-year, full-floor lease for 7,487 square feet at 256 W. 38th Street in Midtown Manhattan after relocating from Philadelphia. The lease represents growing appetite from AI/tech firms seeking well-connected, efficient offices that support collaboration and talent attraction. Brokers note tech companies are diversifying away from trophy towers toward nimble, mid-market spaces.
stories.impact: Tech-driven office demand is stabilizing secondary-grade Manhattan office, but this reflects consolidation and efficiency-seeking, not net job growth into the metro. For multifamily: relocating tech workers from other metros (Philadelphia here) may add incremental demand in close-in neighborhoods (Hudson Yards, Midtown East sublets, Long Island City), but weak signal relative to HQ expansions; monitor whether Treeswift signals broader Philadelphia tech exodus.

stories.title: Van Nuys Apartments Trade for First Time Since Delivery
stories.excerpt: Marcus & Millichap closed the sale of 7203 Rubio Ave., a 30-unit multifamily property in the Lake Balboa neighborhood of Van Nuys. The property sold for $9.5 million or $316,667 per unit. Marcus & Millichap Capital Corporation (MMCC), a subsidiary of Marcus & Millichap, secured $6,223,000 in acquisition financing. “Bringing this property to market for the first time since its construction in 2013 generated significant investor interest,” said Neema Ahadian, senior managing director investments. “After a disciplined marketing process that included eight property tours and five competitive offers, we identified a qualified buyer who performed without requesting price reductions or credits in escrow. The transaction reflects continued demand for well-located, newer-vintage multifamily properties that are not subject to the Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance.”  Ahadian and Leonardo Laterza, investment specialists in Marcus & Millichap’s Los Angeles office, marketed the property on behalf of the seller, a local developer, and procured the buyer, a local private investor. Danny Abergel, executive managing director, capital markets, also based in the firm’s Los Angeles office, secured a five-year loan at 67% loan-to-value with a national bank on behalf of the buyer. Additional terms include a competitive interest rate and a 30-year amortization period. The post Van Nuys Apartments Trade for First Time Since Delivery appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Van Nuys 30-unit property (Lake Balboa, 2013 delivery) sold for $9.5M ($316,667/unit); first trade since construction.
Five competitive offers; buyer avoided price cuts; property exempt from LA Rent Stabilization Ordinance.
Strong demand for newer-vintage, non-RSO-encumbered multifamily in LA; demonstrates investor appetite post-acquisition.
stories.summary: Marcus & Millichap closed the sale of a 30-unit apartment property in Lake Balboa (Van Nuys submarket) for $9.5 million ($316,667 per unit). The 2013-built asset, marketed for the first time since delivery, generated eight property tours and five competitive offers. The buyer, a local private investor, performed without requesting price reductions, signaling strong demand for well-located, newer-vintage multifamily exempt from LA's Rent Stabilization Ordinance.
stories.impact: Investor appetite for non-RSO multifamily in secondary LA submarkets (Valley) remains strong and supports acquisition values, but focus on 2013-vintage ('pre-RSO tightening') suggests scarcity of RSO-exempt product is driving competition. Implication for developers: San Fernando Valley and other Valley submarkets remain acquisition targets; entitlement risk tied to RSO exposure will widen pricing gaps between RSO and non-RSO assets, favoring new or exempt-phase developments.

stories.title: Williamsburg Mixed-Use Sale Completes “Round Trip” for Seller
stories.excerpt: Marcus & Millichap closed the sale of 235-237 Kent Ave., two mixed-use buildings in Brooklyn’s Williamsburg neighborhood, for $16.4 million. “We are happy to successfully complete a round trip for our seller, whom we previously sold the property for $12.3 million in 2021 during the pandemic,” said Shaun Riney of Marcus & Millichap in New York City. “The property is turnkey and located on the world-class corridor of Kent Avenue. The buyer was completing a 1031 exchange following the sale of a property in downtown Manhattan.” Riney, Michael Salvatico and Harrison Rich of Marcus & Millichap marketed the property on behalf of the seller. They also procured the buyer. Built in 1954, the buildings total 13,575 square feet and comprise 14 units, including 12 free-market two-bedroom apartments and two ground-floor commercial spaces. The commercial space is occupied by a restaurant and Ume Sushi. The post Williamsburg Mixed-Use Sale Completes “Round Trip” for Seller appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Williamsburg mixed-use buildings (235-237 Kent Ave., 14 units + 2 commercial) sold for $16.4M; seller's 'round trip' gain.
Originally sold December 2021 at $12.3M during pandemic; resale reflects 33% appreciation in 3.3 years.
Buyer executing 1031 exchange from downtown Manhattan office sale; mixed-use Kent Avenue corridor remains institutional demand anchor.
stories.summary: Marcus & Millichap closed the sale of two 1954-built mixed-use buildings in Williamsburg (235-237 Kent Ave.) for $16.4 million, achieving a 33% gain for the seller from its $12.3 million purchase in December 2021. The 13,575-sq-ft buildings comprise 12 free-market two-bedroom apartments and two ground-floor commercial spaces (restaurant, sushi). The buyer was completing a 1031 exchange from a downtown Manhattan office disposition.
stories.impact: Rising institutional capital rotation from struggling downtown Manhattan office into Williamsburg mixed-use signals both office distress and sustained demand for walkable, mixed-use residential in Brooklyn. Kent Avenue's continued appeal to 1031 exchanges and residential-focused investors suggests strong renter demand and resilience in the neighborhood; developers should consider Williamsburg infill and adaptive reuse opportunities, particularly for residential-dominant mixed-use where office cap-rate compression persists.

stories.title: Locally Based Investors Acquire Encinitas Offices from Family Trust
stories.excerpt: Cushman & Wakefield, along with locally based buyers DMJ Capital Partners, LLC and StoneSteps Real Estate, LLC, announced the acquisition of a multi-tenant office property, located at 169 Saxony Rd. in Encinitas, for $13.5 million. The property was previously held in a family trust, having been owned and operated by the seller and her late father for more than 24 years.The seller was represented by Brooks Campbell, Louay Alsadek, Peter Curry, and Maddie Mawby with Cushman & Wakefield. DMJ Capital Partners and StoneSteps Real Estate represented themselves. “As a sign of the strong investor demand for well-located office properties in San Diego, we received multiple offers from active investors,” said Campbell. Built in 2001, the two-story coastal office asset encompasses 40,270 rentable square feet and was 69% leased at the time of sale. Cushman & Wakefield has been appointed as leasing agent for the property. The post Locally Based Investors Acquire Encinitas Offices from Family Trust appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: DMJ Capital Partners and StoneSteps Real Estate acquire office property (169 Saxony Rd., Encinitas) for $13.5M.
40,270 sq ft, 69% leased at sale; 2001-built; multiple offers received from active investors.
Coastal San Diego office asset shows investor demand despite sector headwinds; well-located offices remain competitive.
stories.summary: Cushman & Wakefield announced the acquisition of a 40,270-sq-ft, two-story office property in Encinitas (San Diego County) by local buyers DMJ Capital Partners and StoneSteps Real Estate for $13.5 million. The 2001-built property was 69% leased and previously held in a family trust for 24+ years. The sale generated multiple competitive offers from institutional investors, signaling continued strength in well-located coastal office assets.
stories.impact: Office fundamentals in coastal San Diego remain resilient relative to national trends, likely supported by biotech, defense, and tourism sectors. For multifamily developers: strong office demand in Encinitas and surrounding North County coastal markets suggests stable employment and wage bases that underpin rental demand; consider acquisition opportunities for multifamily infill or conversion in these submarkets, as office cap rates may compress further relative to multifamily if office-to-residential conversion zoning is viable.

stories.title: Spanish Hotel Operator Buys Chemists’ Club Hotel at 52 East 41st Street for $95M
stories.excerpt: A 107-key hotel in Midtown has traded for roughly $95 million. Eurostars Hotel Company, a Spanish hotel chain managing more than 300 properties globally, has purchased the Chemists’ Club Hotel at 52 East 41st Street from Azora, another Spanish company specializing in large-scale hotel investments, according to a source with knowledge of the deal. Eastdil Secured’s Jeffrey Davis and Scott Ellman arranged the deal for the seller, while it was unclear who repped the buyer. Eastdil declined to comment, while spokespeople for Eurostars and Azora did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The Real Deal first reported the news. It’s unclear when Azora acquired the 14-story hotel a block south of Grand Central Terminal, but the last trade recorded in property records was in 2007, when hotel chain Grupo Hotusa and Losan Hotels bought it for $77 million. Eurostars, which also owns the Eurostars Wall Street hotel at 129 Front Street in the Financial District, is a subsidiary of Grupo Hotusa, so the Midtown property is returning to its previous roots. The property was built around 1910, but not as a hotel. The building was originally the site of the historic headquarters of the Chemists’ Club, a prominent social and dining hub for leading scientists and industry pioneers. The building was later redeveloped by fortuna realty group in 1997 and opened in 2000 as the Dylan Hotel. Last year, it was again heavily redesigned and rebranded, and officially opened as the Chemists’ Club Hotel. The hotel is currently home to Benjamin Steakhouse on the ground floor and features amenities such as a lounge bar, coworking spaces and a fitness center. News of the sale comes after a slew of other hotel sales in Manhattan recently. In June, Meliá Hotels International bought the 12-story hotel at 132-142 West 27th Street in NoMad for $203 million, while Omni Lifestyle Living acquired a Marriott hotel at 21 West 37th Street in Midtown for $39.9 million, also in June. bullets: Eurostars Hotel Company (Spanish chain, 300+ properties) purchases Chemists' Club Hotel (52 East 41st St., Manhattan) for ~$95M.
107-key Midtown hotel; last comparable trade 2007 ($77M); seller was Azora (Spanish hotel investor).
Property returning to Grupo Hotusa (Eurostars parent); consolidation within international hotel ownership; Midtown Manhattan hotel market remains active.
stories.summary: Eurostars Hotel Company, a Spanish hotel chain managing over 300 properties globally, acquired the 107-key Chemists' Club Hotel at 52 East 41st Street in Midtown Manhattan for approximately $95 million from fellow Spanish investor Azora. The 14-story hotel, a block south of Grand Central Terminal, last traded in 2007 for $77 million. Eurostars is a subsidiary of Grupo Hotusa, the property's previous owner, representing a return to the group's portfolio.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily relevance; however, Midtown hotel consolidation and strong transaction volumes signal capital confidence in Manhattan's post-pandemic recovery and visitor/business travel demand. Indirect signal: Midtown's sustained attractiveness to hospitality capital may support multifamily rental demand via employment and visitor spending, but developers should monitor whether hotel supply ramp affects near-term multifamily rental growth in the core Manhattan submarket.

stories.title: Izo Capital Lends $26M on Wyoming Apartments Near Jackson Hole
stories.excerpt: Sundance Properties has sealed $25.6 million of construction financing to bring a multifamily development in Alpine, Wyo., across the finish line, Commercial Observer has learned. Izo Capital supplied the 24-month senior construction loan to fund the completion of Phase 1 of the developer’s planned the Flats at Alpine Junction project comprising 64 units. The debt will support the completion of three additional buildings comprising 48 apartments on top of 16 units that are already completed and leased. Peter Porraro, co-founder and chief investment officer at Izo Capital, said the overall project, which will eventually total 160 units, is set up for success given that it’s 35 miles from Jackson Hole mountain valley, with a number of employers based in the town of Jackson, Wyo. Porraro noted that Alpine also has demand drivers for multifamily with limited supply coupled with a newly opened medical center and a public charter school scheduled to open for the 2026-2027 academic year. “It’s very hard to develop out there, and it’s hard to get the infrastructure,” Porraro told CO of the need for more apartments projects near Jackson Hole. “There’s just no supply and nothing new in the market.” The Flats development has already shown strong leasing momentum, according to Porraro, with the current rental rates helping support underwriting assumptions in the loan for the remaining phases of the project. The first phase is slated for completion next spring. Porraro noted that there is large-scale demand for rental housing for those who work in Jackson Hole given that median home prices in the city are close to $3 million, with townhomes starting at around $1 million. He said the project at 303 Highway also benefits from transportation connectivity that includes direct access to the START Bus system linking Alpine and Jackson. “The demand we’ve experienced from the first completed building reinforces the critical need for new rental housing in Alpine,”
bullets: Izo Capital funds Sundance Properties' $25.6M construction loan for Flats at Alpine Junction (Alpine, Wyo.); 64-unit Phase 1.
Project near Jackson Hole; limited supply, new medical center, and charter school (2026–27) opening drive multifamily demand.
24-month senior construction financing; Phase 1 adds 48 units to 16 completed; ultimate buildout 160 units.
stories.summary: Izo Capital supplied a $25.6 million, 24-month construction loan to Sundance Properties to complete Phase 1 of the Flats at Alpine Junction, a planned 160-unit multifamily development in Alpine, Wyoming, 35 miles from Jackson Hole. The loan funds three buildings totaling 48 additional apartments on top of 16 already completed and leased. Demand drivers include proximity to Jackson employers, a newly opened medical center, and a public charter school opening in 2026–27.
stories.impact: Alpine/Jackson Hole market shows strong fundamentals (employer base, supply constraints, infrastructure growth) and lender appetite for construction capital despite Wyoming's remoteness. Signal: regional markets with limited multifamily supply, anchored by outdoor recreation and professional employment clusters, attract development capital; developers should evaluate similar ski-town and mountain-gateway submarkets (Colorado Front Range, Tahoe region, Sun Valley) where population pressure and local constraints support underserved rental demand.

stories.title: CW Realty Closes Deal to Buy 55 Smith Street in Downtown Brooklyn for $58M
stories.excerpt: CW Realty Group closed on a deal to acquire a parking facility in Downtown Brooklyn, Commercial Observer has learned. Cheskie Weisz’ CW Realty entered into a contract to purchase 55 Smith Street in December from New Jersey-based firm Edison Properties, Crain’s New York Business reported at the time. The sale closed on Friday and its price was disclosed at $58 million, according to broker JLL. CW Realty has not disclosed any specifics about their plans for the site, which has an alternative address of 160 Livingston Street, but the lot spans 13,707 square feet and is one of the biggest residential development opportunities in Downtown Brooklyn, the JLL Capital Markets team said. “This transaction demonstrates the strength of demand for well-located development opportunities across New York City, particularly in neighborhoods with strong residential fundamentals and supportive zoning,” JLL’s Mike Mazzara, who negotiated the deal alongside Ethan Stanton, Brendan Maddigan and Drew Isaacson, said in a statement. “The site offers a combination of scale, flexibility and development incentives in one of Brooklyn’s most dynamic neighborhoods.” CW Realty and Edison Properties did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Developers can build 137,000 square feet on the site as of right or 164,000 square feet under the Universal Affordability Preference program with no height limits or parking requirements for a potential housing development. CW Realty has the option to build using the city’s 485-x program and benefit from reforms made under the City of Yes for Housing Opportunity. An added bonus is that development on the site is not restricted to rental housing or condominiums, according to JLL. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: CW Realty Group acquires parking facility (55 Smith Street / 160 Livingston, Downtown Brooklyn) for $58M; closed Friday.
13,707-sq-ft lot; described as one of largest residential development opportunities in Downtown Brooklyn; zoning supportive.
JLL notes strong demand for development sites in Brooklyn with strong residential fundamentals and flexible zoning.
stories.summary: CW Realty Group closed on the acquisition of a parking facility at 55 Smith Street (also 160 Livingston Street) in Downtown Brooklyn for $58 million. The 13,707-sq-ft lot is positioned as one of the largest remaining residential development opportunities in the submarket. JLL Capital Markets, which brokered the deal, highlighted strong demand for well-located development sites in neighborhoods with supportive zoning and residential demand fundamentals. CW Realty has not disclosed redevelopment plans.
stories.impact: Large-format development site acquisition in prime Downtown Brooklyn signals confidence in submarket fundamentals and scarcity of entitled or shovel-ready parcels. Implication: Downtown Brooklyn's supply-constrained pipeline and sustained rental demand make assemblies and parking-to-residential conversions attractive; developers should accelerate site control in neighboring pockets and monitor zoning variance/entitlement timelines, as competition for sites will intensify and land costs are rising.

stories.title: Kimco Buys Two Broward Retail Centers for $109M
stories.excerpt: Kimco Realty, one of the biggest owners of grocery-anchored retail centers in the country, has acquired two more in Broward County for a combined $109 million from KPR Centers, property records show. In the largest transaction, the Jericho, N.Y.-based REIT paid $56 million for Sunshine Plaza, a 245,744-square-foot property between 4017 and 4299 West Commercial Boulevard in Tamarac, just east of the Florida’s Turnpike. Publix and Marshalls anchor the 19-acre shopping center. Other tenants include Crunch Fitness, Krispy Kreme and Subway. New York-based KPR had purchased the property for $28.5 million in 2014. In the smaller trade, Kimco Realty paid $53 million for the 254,749-square-foot Pompano Marketplace at 1115 and 1117 South Federal Highway. It also spans about 19 acres, with a Walmart Neighborhood Market as the anchor. Other tenants include Ross Dress for Less, Carrabba’s Italian Grill and TD Bank. KPR Centers had purchased the asset for $46.8 million in 2015. Kimco Realty owns 589 properties nationwide, including 44 across South Florida. In one of South Florida’s largest retail deals in recent years, the REIT paid $216 million for The Shops at Mary Brickell Village in Miami in 2022. Representatives for Kimco Realty and KPR Centers did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Kimco Realty acquires two Broward grocery-anchored retail centers from KPR Centers for combined $109M.
Sunshine Plaza (Tamarac): $56M for 245,744 sq ft (Publix/Marshalls); Pompano Marketplace: $53M for 254,749 sq ft (Walmart Neighborhood Market).
KPR had purchased assets 2014–15 for $28.5M and $46.8M respectively; Kimco's REIT-scale acquisition reflects consolidation and yield-seeking.
stories.summary: Kimco Realty acquired two grocery-anchored retail centers in Broward County from KPR Centers for a combined $109 million. Sunshine Plaza in Tamarac sold for $56 million (245,744 sq ft, Publix/Marshalls anchored); Pompano Marketplace sold for $53 million (254,749 sq ft, Walmart Neighborhood Market anchored). Both properties had been held by KPR since 2014–15 and sold at material premiums to original acquisition costs, reflecting strong grocery-retail valuations and REIT consolidation trends.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily impact; however, Kimco's active acquisition of necessity-based retail in suburban South Florida signals confidence in regional demographics and consumer spending. Indirect: strong suburban retail valuations and REIT capital deployment in grocery-anchored centers may crowd out development capital for multifamily in competing Broward submarkets, but reinforce that suburban South Florida population and household formation remain resilient, supporting multifamily fundamentals in surrounding areas.

stories.title: Schuckman Buys Northeast Queens Shopping Center for $56M
stories.excerpt: Punia & Marx Real Estate sold the Whitestone Shopping Center in Queens for $56 million. BTF Capital Fund, led by Kenneth Schuckman and Aaron Malinsky, purchased the Key Food-anchored property at 153-15 Cross Island Parkway, according to a deed transfer in property records filed Friday. The purchase could be a play for assets tied to grocery stores and other necessity-based retail. Schuckman’s brokerage firm, Schuckman Realty, will handle leasing for the shopping center, according to the buyer. Acadia Realty Trust provided about $48.5 million in financing to Schuckman for the acquisition through a shell corporation, with Acadia’s Chief Financial Officer John Gottfried signing the mortgage documents. Punia & Marx and Acadia did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Punia & Marx has owned the property since at least 1975, and the amount paid for that acquisition is unknown. Schuckman seems to have been involved in the management operations of the 220,000-square-foot shopping center, which is also leased to a Chase Bank branch, with a 2020 flier listing Kenneth Schuckman and Jessica Vilmenay as exclusive brokers. The advertisement said at the time that a redevelopment of the property would be taking place, but was not specific about the nature of the repositioning. Schuckman promoted the center based on 100,000 cars passing by the center daily on the Cross Island Parkway and 333,000 people living within three miles. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: BTF Capital Fund (Schuckman, Malinsky) acquires Whitestone Shopping Center (Queens; Key Food-anchored) for $56M.
220,000-sq-ft property; 153-15 Cross Island Parkway; Punia & Marx seller (owned since ≥1975).
Acadia Realty Trust financed acquisition with ~$48.5M loan; Schuckman Realty to handle leasing; grocery/necessity retail consolidation play.
stories.summary: BTF Capital Fund, led by Kenneth Schuckman and Aaron Malinsky, acquired the Whitestone Shopping Center in Queens for $56 million from long-time holder Punia & Marx (owned since 1975 or earlier). The 220,000-sq-ft property is anchored by Key Food and located at 153-15 Cross Island Parkway. Acadia Realty Trust provided approximately $48.5 million in financing. Schuckman Realty will manage leasing for the center.
stories.impact: Grocery-anchored retail consolidation in Queens signals investor appetite for necessity-based retail in outer-borough submarkets and suburban-proximate locations. For multifamily: continued strength in grocery/necessity retail valuations in Queens (and other outer boroughs) indicates stable household formation and spending power; developers should target infill multifamily adjacent to or near grocery-anchored centers and transit nodes, as these retail anchors stabilize demographics and renter profiles in neighborhoods.
